questions.q: In the atrial-enlargement approach, an abnormal P wave localises the primary waveform abnormality to which origin?
questions.exp: The atrial-enlargement section identifies abnormal P waves with pathology of atrial origin. (Book p383)

questions.q: A patient with COPD has tall, peaked, pointed P waves. Which pairing matches this section?
questions.exp: Pointed P is P-pulmonale and indicates right atrial enlargement; tall, peaked P waves are associated with COPD. (Book p383)

questions.q: With an atrial-origin rhythm, which rate crosses the printed threshold for atrial tachycardia?
questions.exp: The rate threshold printed here is greater than 100 bpm, not merely equal to 100. (Book p383)

questions.q: The right-atrial-enlargement figure groups pointed P-wave panels in ____ alongside a V1 panel.
questions.exp: The labelled small panels are II, III, aVF and V1; the inferior panels and the marked full tracing illustrate P-pulmonale/right atrial enlargement. (Book p383)

questions.q: A bifid rather than pointed P wave is identified. What is the book’s atrial-enlargement interpretation?
questions.exp: Left atrial enlargement produces a bifid P wave, called P-mitrale. (Book p383)

questions.q: Which panel set belongs to the left-atrial-enlargement illustration, showing bifid P waves and a prominent terminal negative component in V1?
questions.exp: The left-atrial-enlargement panels are labelled I, II, aVF and V1; arrows/circles in the accompanying ECG draw attention to the abnormal P waves. (Book p383)

questions.q: Complete the note’s corrected-QT equation: QTc = ____.
questions.exp: The note gives QTc = QT divided by the square root of RR. (Book p383)

questions.q: The LVH axis line places the leftward axis between ____ (the aVL angle is printed without a minus sign on this page).
questions.exp: The line gives aVL (printed 30°) to lead I (0°), called leftward axis. The conventional aVL angle is −30°, as on p382; the missing sign is a source discrepancy. (Book p383)

questions.q: True or false: LVH pushes the net vector leftward because left-sided muscle mass increases.
opts: True — right-sided muscle mass increases and reverses the septal vector
False — increased left mass pushes the vector rightward
False — hypertrophy changes PR duration but not the net vector
True — the increased left mass pulls the net vector leftward
questions.exp: The LVH flowchart links increased left muscle mass to a vector pushed to the left. (Book p383)

questions.q: The LVH tracing highlights large leftward forces. Which polarity pair follows the printed explanation?
opts: Larger positive left-sided and larger negative right-sided deflections
Larger positive deflections on both sides
Larger negative left-sided and larger positive right-sided deflections
Larger negative deflections on both sides
questions.exp: LVH increases positive deflections on the left and negative deflections on the right; the ECG is captioned left ventricular hypertrophy. (Book p383)

questions.q: The precordial Sokolow–Lyon expression printed here is ____.
opts: S in V5 or V6 + S in V1 or V2
R in V5 or V6 + R in V1 or V2
R in V5 or V6 + S in V1 or V2
R in V1 or V2 + S in V5 or V6
questions.exp: The expression adds the lateral R wave (V5 or V6) to the anterior S wave (V1 or V2), rather than swapping the wave types or lead groups. (Book p384)

questions.q: Under the book’s Sokolow–Lyon rule, R in V5 is 23 mm and S in V1 is 13 mm. Which interpretation fits?
opts: Sum 36 mm — proves RVH using an R/S cutoff
Sum 36 mm — exceeds the >35 mm LVH cutoff
Sum 36 mm — below a >40 mm LVH cutoff
Difference 10 mm — fails a >11 mm precordial cutoff
questions.exp: The book adds R in V5 or V6 to S in V1 or V2 and uses >35 mm for LVH. Here 23 + 13 = 36 mm. (Book p384)

questions.q: The alternative aVL voltage criterion for LVH is ____.
questions.exp: The second printed Sokolow–Lyon line is aVL >11 mm → LVH. (Book p384)

questions.q: Which combination explains the secondary ST/T changes listed with LVH?
opts: Primary PR shortening from aortic stenosis or chronic hypertension
Atrial repolarisation from mitral stenosis or SA exit block
Pressure-overload strain from aortic stenosis or chronic hypertension
Volume-overload strain from isolated COPD or sinus arrest
questions.exp: Secondary ST/T changes accompany strain/pressure overload, with aortic stenosis and chronic hypertension as the listed examples. (Book p384)

questions.q: Which proposed leftward-axis cause does NOT belong with the book’s LVH/LBBB list?
opts: LVH with increased left-sided positive deflection
Isolated RVH with axis between III and aVF
LVH with increased left muscle mass
questions.exp: The two leftward-axis causes listed are LVH and LBBB; the next section places RVH between III and aVF. (Book p384)

questions.q: The RVH axis is described between ____ and is termed rightward.
questions.exp: RVH is placed between lead III at 120° and aVF at 90°, a rightward axis. (Book p384)

questions.q: A tracing with rightward axis has R taller than S in V1 and secondary ST changes in a patient with mitral stenosis. Which printed combination fits?
opts: LBBB — V1 R/S >1, isolated P-wave changes with MS
LVH — V1 R/S <1, secondary ST changes with MS + LVH
RVH — V1 R/S <1, primary PR changes with MS
RVH — V1 R/S >1, secondary ST changes with MS + RVH
questions.exp: The RVH section specifies V1 R/S >1 and secondary ST changes due to mitral stenosis plus RVH; its tracing is captioned RVH. (Book p384)

questions.q: For the P-pulmonale highlighted in the COPD tracing, which lead set and most-common association are listed?
questions.exp: P-pulmonale is listed in II, III and aVF, most commonly with COPD; those inferior P waves are circled in the figure. (Book p384)

questions.q: Which sequence reproduces the COPD axis flowchart?
opts: Hyperinflated lung → diaphragm pushed upward → axis shifts to 120°
Hyperinflated lung → diaphragm pushed downward → axis shifts to −30°
Hyperinflated lung → diaphragm pushed upward → axis shifts to 0°
Hyperinflated lung → diaphragm pushed downward → axis shifts to 90°
questions.exp: The flowchart runs COPD → hyperinflated lung → downward push of diaphragm → axis shifts to 90°. (Book p384)

questions.q: At the end of that flowchart, prominent complexes occur in ____, while absent complexes in ____ define the lead I sign.
questions.exp: The two arms are prominent complexes in aVF and II, and absent complexes in I, called the lead I sign. (Book p384)

questions.q: Which finding contradicts the four ECG signs of COPD listed here?
opts: Poor R-wave progression from V1 to V6
Wide QRS as the listed baseline QRS feature
questions.exp: The listed signs are narrow QRS, poor R progression V1–V6, P-pulmonale and a positive lead I sign. (Book p384)

questions.q: In the book’s RVH-with-RBBB example, R/S >1 accompanies an axis between I and aVL. What combined enlargement is inferred?
opts: No hypertrophy — RR′ alone explains the axis
Biventricular hypertrophy — RVH plus leftward axis
Isolated RVH — leftward axis excludes LVH
questions.exp: The example labels R/S and RR′, assigns R/S >1 to RVH and I–aVL to leftward axis, then calls RVH plus leftward axis biventricular hypertrophy. (Book p385)

questions.q: Match the RBBB morphology call-outs — 1) V1 terminal force 2) V6 terminal force 3) Blocked branch in the cartoon … A) Right bundle branch B) Wide S wave C) R′ wave
questions.exp: The RBBB cartoon marks the right bundle. V1 variants rr′, RR′ and rsR′ share terminal R′; V6 qRS/RS variants share a wide terminal S. (Book p385)

questions.q: The morphology figure places ____ in V1 and ____ in V6.
opts: rS / QS; broad isolated R only
Broad isolated R only; rS / QS
questions.exp: The labelled RBBB panels give rr′, RR′, rsR′ in V1 and qRS, RS in V6. (Book p385)

questions.q: Match the first three fascicular-classification lines — 1) RBBB alone 2) RBBB plus LAFB or LPFB 3) LBBB alone … A) Bifascicular combination with a left fascicular block B) Bifascicular block by itself C) Unifascicular block
questions.exp: The book calls RBBB alone unifascicular, RBBB with either left fascicular block bifascicular, and LBBB bifascicular by itself. (Book p385)

questions.q: True or false: the next line calls bifascicular block plus increased PR interval or Mobitz block trifascicular.
opts: True — but only a shortened PR satisfies that line
False — only isolated RBBB is labelled trifascicular
False — the line instead calls this unifascicular
True — that is the printed classification
questions.exp: The line says bifascicular block + increased PR interval/Mobitz block = trifascicular. This is source terminology; prolonged PR alone does not prove disease of the remaining fascicle. (Book p385)

questions.q: For LBBB, the text gives an I–aVL leftward axis and asks you to inspect ____ for LBBB morphology.
questions.exp: The LBBB bullets give I–aVL leftward axis and V5, V6, aVL morphology; the adjacent tracing marks LVH and lateral LBBB features. (Book p385)

questions.q: Match the LBBB figure’s morphology and conduction panels — 1) V1 rS / QS variants 2) V6 broad R / RR′ variants 3) Cartoon with left-sided conduction interruption … A) Left bundle branch block B) W pattern C) M pattern
questions.exp: The left-bundle cartoons accompany a V1 W-pattern row and a V6 M-pattern row; the latter includes both notched RR′ and broad R forms. (Book p385)

questions.q: Which timing pair agrees with the LBBB figure’s small-print call-outs?
opts: R-peak time >0.16 s in both V1 and V6
R-peak time normal in V1; prolonged >0.05 s in V6
R-peak time >0.05 s in V1; normal in V6
R-peak time normal in V1; prolonged >0.12 s in V6
questions.exp: The figure labels onset of intrinsicoid deflection (R-peak time) normal in V1 and prolonged in V6, measuring >0.05 seconds. (Book p385)

questions.q: The Sgarbossa section addresses diagnosis of which combination?
questions.exp: Its stated purpose is to diagnose MI along with LBBB. (Book p385)

questions.q: Match the three ST-change descriptions in the text — 1) V1 or V2, concordant change 2) V1 or V2, discordant change 3) V5 or V6, concordant change … A) ST depression B) ST elevation with the QRS C) ST elevation opposite the QRS
questions.exp: The text lists concordant ST depression and discordant ST elevation in V1/V2, and concordant ST elevation in V5/V6. (Book p385)

questions.q: Which pair reproduces numbered panels 1 and 2?
opts: Concordant elevation >5 mm with positive QRS; concordant depression >5 mm in V1–V3
Concordant elevation >1 mm with positive QRS; concordant depression >1 mm in V1–V3
Discordant elevation >1 mm with positive QRS; concordant depression >5 mm in V5–V6
Concordant depression >1 mm with positive QRS; discordant elevation >1 mm in V1–V3
questions.exp: Panel 1 labels concordant ST elevation >1 mm with positive QRS; panel 2 labels concordant ST depression >1 mm in V1–V3. (Book p385)

questions.q: At the labelled J point, discordant ST elevation is 5 mm and preceding S depth is 15 mm. Which calculation matches panel 3?
questions.exp: The figure divides J-point discordant STE height (5 mm) by preceding S-wave height (15 mm): 0.33, above 0.25 or 25%. This proportional panel is distinct from the absolute >5 mm criterion on the next page. (Book p385)

questions.q: Match each textual criterion to its lead group and threshold — 1) Concordant ST elevation 2) Discordant ST elevation 3) Concordant ST depression … A) V1/V2, >5 mm B) V1/V2, >1 mm C) V5/V6, >1 mm
questions.exp: The three textual criteria use strict > thresholds: lateral concordant elevation >1 mm, V1/V2 discordant elevation >5 mm and V1/V2 concordant depression >1 mm. (Book p386)

questions.q: In the V1–V3 morphology panels, which pair is labelled LBBB + acute MI rather than LBBB without MI?
opts: Concordant ST elevation only in aVL or isolated P-mitrale
Concordant ST depression ≥1 mm or abnormally discordant elevation ≥5 mm
Ordinary discordant elevation or concordant depression <1 mm
Ordinary discordant depression or an isolated tall R in V1
questions.exp: The left panel group contrasts ordinary discordant ST in LBBB without MI against concordant ST ≥1 mm and abnormally discordant ST ≥5 mm in LBBB + acute MI. These diagram labels use ≥, whereas the prose above uses >. (Book p386)

questions.q: True or false: the V5, V6, II, III and aVF panels label concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm as LBBB + acute MI, in contrast to the no-MI discordant pattern.
opts: False — those panels are labelled V1, V2 and V3
True — the no-MI panel also requires concordant elevation ≥1 mm
True — concordance and ≥1 mm identify the acute-MI panel
False — only discordant depression ≥5 mm is labelled acute MI
questions.exp: The right-hand group is labelled V5, V6, II, III, aVF and contrasts discordant ST in LBBB without MI with concordant ST ≥1 mm in LBBB + acute MI. (Book p386)

questions.q: The two bottom annotated ECGs are captioned, from left to right, ____ and ____.
opts: LBBB without MI, concordant elevation >1 mm; ordinary discordant elevation <5 mm
Acute MI with LBBB, concordant elevation >1 mm; discordant elevation >5 mm
Acute MI with LBBB, discordant elevation >5 mm; concordant depression >1 mm
LVH, concordant elevation >5 mm; RVH, discordant elevation >1 mm
questions.exp: The arrows and circles on the left mark concordant elevation >1 mm in acute MI with LBBB; the right caption is discordant elevation >5 mm. (Book p386)

units.title: Atrial Enlargement & Corrected QT
units.guide:
Distinguish pointed P-pulmonale from bifid P-mitrale using the labelled lead panels.
Keep atrial origin, tachycardia rate and the corrected-QT equation separate.

units.title: LV Hypertrophy & Leftward Axis
units.guide:
Follow increased left muscle mass through vector displacement and lead polarity.
Then apply both printed Sokolow–Lyon cutoffs and the pressure-overload association.

units.title: RV Hypertrophy, P-pulmonale & COPD
units.guide:
Separate RVH voltage and axis clues from the COPD axis mechanism.
Trace hyperinflation to the lead I sign, then recognise all four listed COPD findings.

units.title: Bundle Branch Blocks & Fascicular Patterns
units.guide:
Read the RVH-with-RBBB example before the fascicular classification.
Compare RBBB terminal forces with the LBBB W/M panels and R-peak timing.

units.title: Sgarbossa Criteria & MI Panels
units.guide:
Use concordance, lead group and magnitude together when reading the book’s LBBB/MI examples.
Distinguish the text’s strict inequalities from the panels’ inclusive labels and the proportional criterion.
